message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
The pilot itself looks well run, and the arithmetic in Table 2 is correct. But the study's three main conclusions don't hold up against its own figures:
- **Participation was not similar across housing types.** Flats took part at about a third of the rate of houses.
- **The tonnage projection uses a participation rate the pilot never recorded**, so the tonnage and the disposal saving are overstated.
- **Brookfield can take only about half of the projected tonnage.** Once that is accounted for, the service is not fully funded.

## 1. Flats participated at a third of the rate of houses

Table 1 shows 66% participation for houses and 21% for flats. The text calls this "broadly similar" and uses it to justify a uniform service. That is the opposite of what the data show.

Flats are about 20% of the district, roughly 10,400 households. Low participation in flats is a common problem with food waste services, usually addressed with communal containers, different collection points and targeted communications. The statutory requirement covers flats too. The study should propose an approach for flats, or at least plan for one, rather than conclude none is needed.

## 2. The projection uses 64%, but the pilot measured 57%

The 64% figure in section 3 doesn't appear in the pilot results. The pilot's overall rate was 57%. The pilot was also 20% flats, the same share as the district, so the pilot's overall figures should transfer to the district directly.

Using the actual rates for each housing type:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ~2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ~160 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **~2,870** |

That is about **2,870 tonnes, not 3,290**. The disposal saving falls to about **£212,000** (2,870 × £74), not £243,000.

## 3. Brookfield's capacity covers only about 60% of the tonnage

Brookfield has confirmed only **1,800 tonnes a year** until 2029. That leaves about **1,070 tonnes a year** (on the corrected figure) with nowhere costed to go. The alternative is a plant 46 miles away. That brings:
- an unknown gate fee;
- haulage costs, or longer vehicle trips that take time away from collection rounds;
- possibly a need for a transfer arrangement.

None of this is costed. Section 4 even calls Brookfield "local" for all the tonnage.

Two further points:
- Brookfield "can offer" capacity, which is not the same as a signed contract. The vehicle order shouldn't go ahead before the treatment contract is secured.
- Collected food waste can't simply go back to incineration. Separately collected food waste must be recycled, so the overflow has to be treated somewhere.

## 4. The service is not fully funded

The study's own cost total, with the corrected saving, already exceeds the allocation:

> £733,400 − £212,000 ≈ **£521,000** net cost, against a provisional allocation of £520,000.

That is before the overflow tonnage, haulage, or any of the missing costs below. The allocation is also only "provisional", and the Government has merely "indicated" funding will be provided. The study should say whether it is confirmed, how long it lasts, and whether it covers start-up costs.

## 5. The cost table is not complete

Likely omissions:
- **On-costs for staff.** If £34,000 is salary only, employer National Insurance and pension add roughly a quarter.
- **Cover for absence.** There is no allowance for agency or relief staff during annual leave and sickness. Six crews with no slack can't cover a weekly service.
- **A spare vehicle.** Six vehicles for six rounds means any breakdown or service visit causes missed collections.
- **Supervision and management**, plus depot space and parking.
- **Financing.** Straight-line depreciation ignores the cost of borrowing £990,000.
- **The dedicated phone line and web page** described in section 6.
- **Upfront cash.** Caddies for 52,000 households are delivered in March 2027 and paid for up front, even though the table spreads them over several years.
- **Round capacity.** The study gives no workload per round. Six vehicles covering 52,000 households a week means about 1,700 households per vehicle per day, before time spent driving to Brookfield. The pilot should have productivity data to confirm whether six vehicles are enough.

## 6. Smaller points

- **The pilot ran for six months, January to June.** Participation often falls as the novelty wears off, and food waste volumes vary by season. Projecting a full year from the first six months is optimistic.
- **The 81% satisfaction figure** comes from "surveyed pilot households". The study should give the response rate and say whether non-participants were included. Satisfied participants are more likely to respond.
- **The timetable has no slack.** Vehicles are ordered in December for delivery in March, crews are recruited from February, and caddies go to 52,000 households in March. The study needs a contingency if vehicle delivery slips.

## Your description against the document

| Your description | The document shows |
|---|---|
| "Participation held up across houses and flats" | 66% for houses against 21% for flats |
| Projections based on how residents actually behave | The projection uses 64%, which the pilot didn't measure |
| "Every cost line is shown" | Several significant lines are missing (section 5 above) |
| "Treatment is local" | Only for 1,800 of about 2,870 tonnes |
| Net cost "fully covered" | The corrected net cost already exceeds £520,000 before overflow costs |

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct the description of flats in section 2, and add a separate approach for flats or a costed option for one.
2. Project tonnage from the participation rates for each housing type: about 2,870 tonnes and a £212,000 saving.
3. Cost the treatment of tonnage above 1,800 tonnes, and secure the Brookfield contract before ordering vehicles.
4. Complete the cost table, including staff on-costs, absence cover, a spare vehicle, supervision, financing and the helpline.
5. Restate the funding position honestly. On current figures there is a gap, and it should be quantified rather than described as "fully funded".
6. Base vehicle numbers on the pilot's round productivity, including travel time to treatment.

The roll-out itself is required by law, so the question for Cabinet is not whether to go ahead but on what terms. A revised study that shows the true net cost and the arrangements for flats and overflow tonnage will be far stronger than one that will be contradicted by the first year's figures.
